projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Orlando Kelch was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Orlando Bud Kelch. Mr. Kelch served in the U.S. Army Air Corps. He served in the Pacific and his highest rank was T-3. I'm Tom Swope and this recording was made at Mr. Kelch's son's home in Grafton, Ohio, on December 26th, 2002. Bud was 80 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: I was living in Urbana and was -- graduated from high school in 1942 in June and two months later I was in 1-A classification and I was inducted in Cincinnati, Ohio, November the 6th, 1942 and went across the river to Fort Thomas, Kentucky, and we were there for three or four days for classification and physicals and so forth and then we went on a troop terrain to Miami Beach, Florida, for basic training. And from the basic training they divided us up into groups. And I had been in the Boy Scouts for years and years with my two brothers and we were brought up in a children's home, all three of us, and we had a real good scout troop so we all liked signaling and Morse code and all of that and went out to the Camp Breezy, we were always first.

So when I got into the Army there in Miami Beach, they put us in a room, a lot of us, and put earphones on us and played the Morse code, give us some different letters and numbers, and then you were to say whether that was this or that or whether one number sounded like the rest. So then I was -- I knew all the Morse code, so they had me right away, you see. So I was put into Signal Corps and sent to Valparaiso, Indiana, a civilian radio school, and they had probably 50 of us guys were studying to be radio mechanics and 50 would be radio operators and we were stationed right at the edge of a little town of Alto at an old factory that made glass and they had cleaned it out and rigid it up and they were just a big long room with cots in it and we had showers and so forth and then we marched into the little town and ate all of our meals in the restaurant and went to radio school there for three or four months.

And it was pretty nerve racking. We would take Morse code all day. We had to take some mechanics also in case something happened to your radio mechanic that was stationed with you, but it was pretty nerve racking. And when you got out of there, you knew the Morse code. But we took code so fast that we had to use a regular typewriter and type it on a code typewriter but then we got overseas in active duty and then we never had to take more than 10, 15 words a minute, so it was pretty good training.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any really memorable incidents during your training?

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Oh, not particularly. There wasn't too much to do up there. And we would get invited to the people in the little town of Alto, which I'm sure now is quite a lot larger, but on the weekends quite often they would invite us, maybe three or four us to their homes and for dinner on Sundays especially. And it was more or less all work there. We didn't get any -- no place to play ball or anything like that. We were strictly there for training. And so from there we were shipped back to Drew Field, Florida, and eventually assigned to different units and I was assigned to a signal air warning battalion, which had radar, which is during the World War was top secret. So when we got assigned to a unit, there was, oh, a company, each company was made up of five platoons and each platoon had, oh, like 48 to 50 fellas in it, and we were assigned radar units and then there was radar operators, there was -- three or four other fellas in the platoon would be truck drivers, five or six maybe, mechanics, we had two cooks, two cooks' helpers, three medics.

I was chief radio operator, and eventually I got the rank of tech sergeant, which was the highest in the radio division, and then I had, like, seven or eight radio operators under me. And when we were assigned to a radar unit there at Drew Field, why eventually we ended up going out on maneuvers, we would go out into the boondocks and hacked the palmetto full of rattlesnakes, put up your tents, set up your radar unit, camouflage it, camouflage -- we had four, oh, .50 caliber water-cooled guns that we had to put in and placement around it and camouflage those, but it was always top secret so anyplace we went with that unit, when we would move from one town to the next or from a pine woods maybe 50 mile to a hilly area and set up our unit again, it always had to be loaded guns. Every one -- the guns were all loaded.

We went through a little town and every intersection there was a fellow standing with a gun because it was top secret. And even when we set the units up, they had to have 24-hour guard on them. So it was quite an experience being hooked up with that. And needless to say, everyone in the unit was checked by FBI for security, you know, your whole family. So it was quite an experience. And then we went from Florida. We were shipped to Hattiesburg Air Force Base in Mississippi, we were there for a couple of months, we took basic infantry training and had to go through all of the training, more or less, not the regular infantry went through, and we eventually ended up on a troop train going to California, Camp Pinedale in Fresno, California, which was a regular Signal Corps camp, and once we got there, this was like in, oh, the fall of 1943, and they would take each platoon, like I said, which consisted of 40 some men and all we needed was water and food and we had a contained unit.

We had our cooks, and like I said, medics and the radio operators and everything we needed and they would send one platoon maybe out in the desert and the other platoon would be 60, 70, 80 miles away in a heavy wooded area, some would be in the mountains and we kept in track with each other by radio and we slept in pup tents. I had to sleep with the radio mechanic because if anything went wrong with the radio, he and I were right there in the same pup tent. So we would be in the mountain sometimes and the deserts, out in the desert. Especially I remember we ran in the Mohabi Desert for a period of a couple of weeks and then in the daytime it was so hot that you walked around in your shorts and we had to wear heavy high boots because there was too many snakes and cactus, too.

And at night -- at times it would snow at night and they finally brought bails of straw out and we would put it around the bottom of our pup tenants because it got so cold at night, but then by noon the next day, you would be walking around in your shorts, so that was quite an experience. But we did that all for a couple of months in California and then at different times they would have maneuvers and we would have attacks, simulated attacks by fighter planes coming other trying to locate us and we would, of course, jump in our gun pits and train our -- we had these .50 caliber water-cooled guns, you had to crank water with them -- through them to keep them cooled, and if they spotted you, they would come over and spray some sort of liquid stinky stuff all over you, so it was -- that was your punishment for not camouflaging your unit well enough. And it really smelled to the high heaven.

You had to wash everything down. But we had talked about that at our Army reunions quite often about such things as that, that smelly stuff that they would spray on us. But it was good training and we ended up eventually -- we had about three of these maneuvers we went on and then there was times the infantry was hooked up with us, and we ended up going overseas, I think, oh, let's see what the devil the date was. Oh, goodness...

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What were your particular responsibilities as a chief radio operator?

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Well, as chief radio operator, of course, you had to make sure -- you see, we had two radio sets. Once we got overseas, we had two radio sets. One was used for what they call voice. You could talk. And then the other one was used strictly with -- for code, Morse code, which was hooked up with the radar. When the radar would pick up on what they call a blip coming in, it was mapped and the boys in the radar van would read what zones they were in and so forth, and this was all radioed in to Clark Field where they had what they called the plotting room.

And you've seen pictures of these great big flat wooden boards with these things they moved around like airplanes. They kept track of all of the planes that were in the air, especially our unit, because we were on the China Sea, and this was all plotted and it was all coded, that was. And then, of course, to keep the Japanese from picking it up, every so often, I don't remember, they would send me a message and we had a machine that looked like the old check writers where you had a bunch of gears and cogs in it, and you would open it up and you would set these dials to certain numbers they would tell you, and then that scrambled your message up, you see, so the Japanese couldn't have picked it up and read it.

And that was one of my jobs, was to take care of that, and then, of course, to see that we had men on duty all the times and the radios were working right, and that they didn't goof up. And we had, oh, a couple of fellas in the platoon, I remember over in the Philippines, they would be sending a message and at the end of the message one of them would go doot, doot, da-doot-doot on his key on his radio and then the other guy at the other end would go doot-doot. They'd doot, doot, da-doot-doot, doot-doot. Well, they thought that was funny and I didn't, but if I wasn't there watching them all the time, it happened -- and I ended up getting a letter from a commanding general about that, that the Japanese would pick us up and finally locate us and you would be in trouble, you see.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They'd be coming for ya?

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, right. So we went -- we were shipped overseas the first part of April. I think it was April the 6th, '44, we were shipped overseas to New Guinea on a converted liberty ship which was just a transport ship and you were down in the hulls, they had three different levels and each level was made up of wooden planks put in to make it three floors and they had just canvas bunks. And talking about things I remembered, going over we were standing on the rail of the ship watching the Golden Gate Bridge and the skyline disappear, and it was pretty -- it's pretty hard to talk about. But anyway, we would bet who would get seasick first and was quite -- some never did and some never got on it and got over.

We were on the boat 28 days going to New Guinea unescorted and the first three days out they had a Navy blimp flying over us watching for subs because going out of San Francisco Harbor, everything was channeled in, so it would be just like railroad tracks and, you know, Japanese subs, which were in the area, they could get you maybe, and they had these blimps watching us. And then after about three days we were on our own. And I can definitely remember we would be out, way, way out in the ocean and a boat would actually turn around and go the other direction. And I'm thinking what the devil is coming off.

So what they were trying to do is, you know, keep -- throw subs off is what they were trying to do. And the other time we went, we were way down in the South Pacific and we went in between a couple of islands, which I know wasn't a shipping route but evidently they'd gotten information that there were subs in the area, so this troop ship or converted liberty ship we were on actually went between islands so close that we were standing on deck and it looked like you could jump right onto the shoreline and the natives were -- I mean, just had grass shacks and running around with underwear tops on, no bottoms, and that's how close we were to shore.

And the whole land, you could hear the engines rumbling, and so they evidently got hung up on the bottom somewhere, but we all figured that they were trying to get away from the subs. But anyway, we were there, like, 28 days, I think, and we landed at Lae, New Guinea, which was the capital of Dutch New Guinea and there was nothing there, a little narrow strip divided -- the size of a one-lane country road and it had been bombed by the Japs and repaired and bombed again. And there was a couple of cement block buildings. As far as a town there, there was nothing at all. So we were there and we waited and waited and we went up -- they sent us up the valley and our platoon was up on the side of the hill or more or less a half a mountain and we leveled off a place and put up our tents and waited and waited and we wondered what was coming off and finally we were informed that our equipment, a lot of it had been sunk coming over, you see, so we ended up about three -- two or three months in New Guinea waiting.

We were supposed to get into action more or less in the northern part of New Guinea and as it was we missed all of that and our first mess was in Leyte in the Philippines initial landing. So while we were in New Guinea, we sat up on the hill there, our 40 or 50 something guys, and we could look down the valley and see a little air strip down there and we'd go down once in awhile and hitch a ride on a plane. And I remember one day a buddy of mine and I got permission from our lieutenant to take a ride on a glider and they were practicing seeing how fast they could get off six or seven, eight of these big gliders with these DC-3 -- well, they were called C-3 cargo planes and we got a ride in one and it was quite a thrill. They lined them all up and then one plane would pull out in front of the glider and they would hook it up and they'd give the signal and they would take up the slack in the tow rope and off you would go and then another plane would pull over in front of the next glider and take off, and it was quite a thrill.

And that kept us busy. And then we made two or three trips up into the jungles to some native villages, strictly natives, and they weren't allowed around the camps at all. We went up there and a few things like that, tried to pick up souvenirs but they were so dirty and filthy and had all kinds of disease, there wasn't much use going up there again. But anyway, we went from New Guinea, they put us on another boat and we ended up right on the equator off the northeast coast of New Guinea, an island called Biak -- B-I-A-K -- and it wasn't more or less, from what I remember, probably a 30-mile diameter, and it was the island of the caves. And we had gotten there not too long after they had liberated it and they had these huge, huge caves and the whole island was practically coral. And we put our tents up. We had these pyramidal tents then where you sleep six fellas in a tent and ours was at the end of the runway and every time the B-24 bombers and that would take off, that coral dust would blow right down the runway and, oh, just like thick smoke right into your tents, so it was quite a thrill.

But the one thing I do remember about Biak, there was one of the caves that was so big that you could actually drive two-and-a-half ton trucks down into it. And the Japs had a hospital, an underground hospital there, and I understand that when the American allied troops took the island, that the Japs wouldn't come out of that, especially that huge, big cave, so they rolled 55 gallon drums of high octane gasoline down into it and then set it afire and it burned them all and suffocated them all. That's the only way they could get them out of there. But we were there, I don't know, maybe a month, and that's where the invasion, part of the invasion for the Island of Leyte in the Philippines was made up.

And Leyte was the first island that MacArthur, General MacArthur had -- were landed on his return to the Philippines. So the big part of the invasion made up there. And we were loaded this time onto an LST, which is a pretty big landing ship. The front end would open up and drop down and drive boats out or trucks out and so forth. So we were on that invasion convoy of Leyte. I don't know how many days it took, I don't quite remember, but we were on there long enough that at that time the Japanese were getting a little desperate and they had started this kamikaze pilot stuff, which was a pilot would know he was going to die, so they would actually end their life by driving their plane right into a ship.

So this convoy is coming into the Philippines, they knew they were going to have a lot of trouble, and the Navy fellas on the LST were on duty so long that they couldn't take it anymore, 24-hour duty with their guns, with their aircraft guns, so some of us fellas in each platoon had to learn how to shoot them and we stood duty on the guns while they got some rest, you see, but we luckily -- we weren't hit with any but we did see -- I vaguely remember seeing, we passed an LST that had been hit and the front half of it sunk and evidently they got the doors closed on the other part of the ship and the back half or maybe back three quarters, I don't remember, was still floating, and we had passed it within, I don't know, oh, five, six, 700 yards.

There were still guys on the deck waving to us but it had been chopped, the front half -- they had lost the front half of the boat. But that was quite a scary thing because they were having a lot of trouble with them at the time. But we went into Leyte in the Philippines and had radar duty there and then it was -- Tacloban was one of the towns and Dolog (ps) was the other. And then from the Leyte we went -- well, they put us on another LST and we went up to -- there is an island called Mindoro, which is probably, you know, a few hundred miles away, and I can remember laying out in the harbor there and the water was absolutely gorgeous blue water, we laid out in the harbor for a few days or a week, I don't know, and they had a -- constantly had a smoke screen over the top so nothing could see us from the air. And I remember, too, they dropped the front end of the LST down and we were diving and swimming out there off the end of the boat about five miles out off of the shore, off of the island of Mindoro. We were out far enough that we could see the fighter planes just barely reflect in the sun when they were taking off.

And from there we went to -- we went into the invasion of Subic Bay, which was then the southwestern tip of the island of Luzon, which is, I think, probably one of the biggest islands in the Philippine chain. And at that time there was a small naval base there at Subic Bay that the U.S. owned, and we went in there with LSTs. And the thing I remembered about that was when they rammed it up on shore, they couldn't get the big doors in the front to open up because there was a Filipino's grass shack there and they had to get it out of there. And the poor old fella that owned it, and the family, they ran out, and it was up on bamboo stilts that had it about six foot off the ground and he was screaming don't tear his house down, and they had to, so they'd give him so long to get stuff out and the only thing he carried out that looked like it was worth anything was an old Singer sewing machine. Yeah, he carried that out, and they bulldozed it over so that they could get the ship unloaded.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So his house was that close to the ocean, to the bay, huh?

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Right on the beach. Right on the beach, Tom, yeah. Right on the beach. And we were there, oh, let's see, all day and that night we got -- we got a few Jap Zeroes came over and scraped us and at night they came over again and we had quite a night. And Dave was talking here a while ago, that was the same night -- yeah, we were there the one night. And when the alarm goes, there was a 155 men -- .155 millimeter howitzers anticraft guns, they called them long Toms because they had a tremendously long barrel mounted on a vehicle with four set of dual tires, I remember that, whenever there was aircrafts spotted, why, they would shoot off three red tracers and that was red alert, so that meant jump in a foxhole or get under cover. So it was dark, and we hadn't been there long enough to know what was in the area and we were visibly unloading because they wanted us out on that point of land about five miles out in the bay there where there was no civilization whatsoever.

They wanted our radar stuck out on that point right now to protect what aircraft we were going to land in there and so forth, and we heard the long Toms go off and we thought, oh, my God. And we saw this big canvas pile of stuff all covered up about 100 yards away, so I know there was three or four of us at least that ran for that, crawled underneath of there. And anyway, when the air raid was over and the red alert was all cleared, we found out that what we were hiding in and behind was boxes of 5,500 pound bombs. It was all ammunition. So that was -- and, of course, when they sound those red alerts, you don't light any flash lights or nothing, so, you know, you had to run in the absolute darkness. And here we were thinking we were protected.

And the one fella with us, his name was Duey Wilson, he was a real religious fella, he would pray -- he prayed on a raid that lasted probably 10 minutes or so, it seemed like it was longer than that, and he was praying all the time. And after we -- the raid was over, we got to looking around and we said, well, your prayers must have helped because anything that lit close to us, we'd been long gone. But they loaded our platoon on a landing boat, small landing boat, probably took -- I don't know how many it would take because we had two to three big vans, maintenance vans and radar vans and other equipment and they took us out to this point of land called Banipakin (ps) Point I think it was and dropped us off the next morning and the CBs -- they had bulldozers and they had to bulldoze a road up over this cliff, which is, oh, a good hundred and something foot tall straight up, just enough land between -- or beach between it in order for us to put up our pup tents and that.

We spent a couple of nights camped out there on the beach and -- until they got their road built up over the top, so we could get this radar unit up on top of there, you see. And that was quite an experience, too. And the wind blew terribly out there. We were out there probably, I don't know, months. A month or six weeks. I don't remember. But they had guerillas, the Filipino guerillas out there with us because we were a good five miles from the base and there was no home -- no Filipino shacks or nothing out there.

And as fast as they were moving, MacArthur's plan was to bypass Japs, you see. Instead of hitting every island, he would pick certain spots and then he'd cut them off and there would be thousands of them cut off from supplies and food and so forth and that's what they were doing there, so we knew that even though we were out there, there was some of them behind us so that we had these Filipino gorillas there with us. And we stayed out there probably for a month or so and did our washing in old tubs, we would build a fire and wash our clothes and every so many days one of them had a landing boat there, they would come out and take the supply sergeant into the bay -- into the little town of Subic, which was nothing but a -- one little street right along the beach with some wooden front stores and tin roofs and that was all that was there. And the one thing I remembered there on Subic was that there was a little lighthouse way out at the end right there where we were and an old two-story wooden house that had been bombed a couple of times when they took it from us, and then we took it back, and the little lighthouse was just big enough for one man to be able to go up in, you couldn't live in it or anything.

So this wooden house, old wooden house there, we decided the roof was too far gone so we camped out on the porch, our radio crew, and we took over that one building and slept out on the porch with our pup or our cots and our mosquito netting over it and -- but at about this time they were getting -- they were trying to take Corregidor Island, which was, oh, probably, I don't know, maybe I'd say 30, 40 miles off in the distance to the east, and at night we would get two or three PT boats that would come out of Subic Bay there and us looking down at them, it looked like they was an inch long from where we were up there and they knew we were there. So we'd watch them and then, oh, give them, I don't know, an hour or so, I don't remember, way off in the distance. What they would do is they would circle Corregidor Island and (? shallot ?), you see, these PT boats, and we could see the flashes like lightening way off in the distance and maybe an hour or so later they would come back.

Well, I had a blinker light fixed up and I would send Morse code to them, you see, and I would ask them, you know, what they did and so forth, so we -- it was -- it got to be something to do in the evening. They knew we weren't Japanese and knew who we were and what we were doing up there, but they kept us informed in what was going on in Corregidor. And I remember the one time, the last thing the guy said was, well, I think that was our last trip, so I figured, well, they had Corregidor, they eventually sent in paratroopers and dropped the paratroopers in before the regular infantry went in. But we were there probably about six weeks maybe, and they loaded our platoon on another one of those landing boats and we went up the west coast of Luzon, a little fishing village called Santa Cruz, and they had a little town square there and there was no other -- nothing along the coast there except -- well, our -- we had four platoons covering the whole west coast of Luzon and we were probably 70 or 80 miles apart and we had, like I said, what, two radios, one of them was voice, we kept in contact with the other platoons, or if we wanted to talk to headquarters or Clark Field, we used the one with the voice on because the other one, the code radio, it was strictly to be used with the radar. Nothing interfered with that at all.

But this little fishing village was just some wooden houses that people had had some money and the superintendent of the schools, they had a wooden house, no paint on it, but a tin roof and, you know, a fairly decent house but nothing like over here, and then the rest of the houses in the little village and along the ocean there, they was just grass shacks and so forth like that. But they didn't allow any of the -- Filipinos were [sic] allowed up there except one young boy came up and everyone seemed to like him so he got to be the messenger, and his name was Basilio Marza -- M-A-R-Z-A -- and real nice kid, and I always thought he was a lot younger than me and then he passed away about, oh, I don't know, maybe ten years ago, and his family sent me a letter and I corresponded with him for quite a few years after the war and Basilio was the same age as I was.

You know, I didn't realize he was that same age that I was. But he eventually -- he was the courier. He was the only one allowed into the camp. And, of course, we had it guarded the whole time. There again, we were up on a high point of land and there had been an old mine, not a mine there but they had a mine box site up in the mountains and they would bring it down before the war and they had a little narrow gauge railroad track that ran out into the bay a little bit and they would load this box right onto these one ship at a time. Other than that, that's all that was there, was a couple of big two-story wooden buildings. And so we took that over as our base.

And Basilio had come in from town, which as I know, a mile and a half, two miles up the beach, and he was our courier, he would take some of our wash in and the women would wash our clothes in the streams because even before the war they didn't have any electricity at all, and then he would take some of the old canned goods we didn't like and he would take it in, trade it, bring us back chickens and eggs and bananas and some fruit and stuff like that. So he was quite a nice kid. But -- Dave made a mention about it, oh, we got into some scrapes with the Japs because they would bypass and some off our platoons, like one of them was stationed in close to Manila, their service was altogether different than ours.

We were out in the country, way out in the remote countryside, no other military outfit other than some of these Filipino gorillas were within 80, 90 miles of us, and so we had to have gorillas with us all the time. And I hate to say it, they did the dirty work, but they had to help. We had to help them, also. But they stayed down at the bottom of the hill down there. There was a gravel road that went up to where our camp site was and they stayed down there and lived down there, they made some bamboo houses and thatched roofs and stayed right down there and our government paid them a little money and feed them and so forth and gave them half uniforms that weren't really uniformed up. But the one day we got word that there was -- well, the Japs were about -- oh, we were probably a couple of miles from the foot hills in the mountains and there was no road from Subic Bay all the way to Lingayen Gulf, which would be may 100, maybe 200 miles long.

There was no road over the mountains at all, and you had to go all the way to Lingayen Gulf and come around the mountain and the gap in the mountain to go to Clark Field. But the Japs bypassed, oh, who knows how many hundreds of them, and they were back in the mountains and they eventually got hungry and they got malaria and stuff like that and got a little brave and they would come down quite often and kill some of the Filipino people back there in these little farms and grass shacks and take their water buffalo and chicken and pigs, whatever, it got to be pretty bad so they radio downed from Lingayen Gulf, the infantry did, and said they would send in a squad, which is usually either 10 infantry men and down, and were to take so many of the gorillas and any of the fellas at our base that had time off and go back because they had to be pushed back and they had information that there was maybe as many as a thousand back there, you see.

Well, here we only had 40 something fellas so you had to do something about it. So I was off duty so I went with them and there was about six of our fellas that went, well, we only had 48 there so we couldn't spare a lot, we had, I don't know, maybe 20 -- 15, 20 gorillas in the squad of infantry, we went back through the -- the rice paddies were dry at this time of the year, and we got back to the foot hills of the mountains there and started up over a ridge, like, which was just grass and some huge boulders, oh, the size of big living room recliner chairs, I remember that, and we started up the hill. And the gorillas knew about where they were. And the idea was as long as they didn't bother you, you left them alone, and that's what the gorillas did, too.

And we started up over the hill and there was a ridge in front of us, oh, a cliff, maybe it was 50, 70, 80 foot tall, I don't know, a lot of vines there, we got up over the top and started down the other side of this slope, which, like I say, it wasn't trees or anything around there but these boulders, they were waiting for us, they opened up on us, and luckily some of the guys got on it -- back on the other side of the hill, some of us did and we got behind the rocks. But this Basilio was with us, this young Filipino boy, and he knew a shortcut back and he ran all the way back into the base, which was a couple of miles, and told the fellas that we were pinned down, we were in trouble, and they loaded up one of these .50 caliber water-cooled anti-aircraft guns we had, well, that's what we used them for, more or less, and put it in the back of a two-and-a-half ton truck with some jugs of water, cans of waters to cool it, and luckily the rice paddies were dry so they could go right through them, and got back there and gave us enough cover, they kept raking the hill and the cliff and got -- we got out of there. But we lost a couple and I think we got two or three Filipino gorillas they lost and one infantry -- the infantry squad leaders, we lost him. But we got into a couple of scrapes like that, but we were lucky.

We were real lucky. We didn't have -- like these infantry guys that go in by the first waves, they're the ones that get into the big trouble. We had trouble with them all the time. But one thing I would want to say is that these Japs get a little crazy. They would get malaria, dengue fever and they didn't know where they were and they'd come down out of the hills and they'd get into the little fishing village, and then the trouble started because they -- we saw so many of those Filipino fellas that the Japanese would accuse them of being look-outs for the American forces, you see, or something, and they would take them into the town square and they had a big old wooden pump in there and a lot of these people didn't have their own water out in these little barrios, villages, and they would come in and get water, but the Japs would bring these Filipino fellas in there that they suspected were collaborating with the Americans and they would put them on the ground and make them drink water and just force them to drink water, put a tube, pipe in their mouth, just fill them full of water, then they would get up about two foot off the ground around -- this pump had, like, a step built around it, they would get up on that and jump out onto their stomach and watch the water fly out of their mouth.

You know, and now we heard this story so many times, we knew it was true, and they'd laugh and carry on. But we saw, I don't know how many now. I probably saw two or three that had -- their tongue had a hole burnt right through the center of it, or they would poke holes through their ears and their eyes, you know, just treated them terrible. But when one of these Japs would come into town, mosey into town all delirious out of his head, most of the time, of course they would grab him and then they would parade him through the little fishing village, whipped him, spit on him, throw anything they had on him, but they'd end up bringing him out to our camp where we were and they wanted to show us what they was going to do to him.

Well, there was nothing we could do. You know, it wasn't -- he didn't hurt us, he hurt them. But they'd tie him to a stake, make him dig his own grave and go back about, oh, maybe 50 yards and had his hands tied behind him and he usually had just a little white loin cloth on and they would strip all of his clothes off of him and take him about 50 yards away, drive a bamboo -- big bamboo peg into the ground, tied his arms behind him to the peg and then get off in front of him four, five, six or eight of them, I don't remember, and shoot him and then run up and see who could get to him first because they pulled his gold teeth out.

And the Japanese always had a lot of gold teeth, I remember that very well. And you just think now, you know, well, what can you do? You know what they did to them, you see, so they had a chance to give it back to them and no one told us to stop it. So it happened probably I would say -- we were there probably eight months. It probably happened half a dozen times anyway. Yeah, it just -- then they would drag him back and throw him in a hole he dug and throw gasoline on him and burn him. So that's -- but we have our Army reunions every year and we never have more than two or three dozen show up anymore. Most of them are dead. But we talked about things like that. And some of the platoons that ran in the bigger towns like Manila and those towns, they didn't get to see anything like that, you see, but we were out there all by ourselves and isolated and we would run into quite a few things like that that they didn't get to see at all.

But when the war was over, of course we got notification that at a certain time at a certain day this plane would fly from Japan to Clark Field and it would be marked a certain way, it had a big red cross on the side. It was a transport plane. But we actually saw it come right over our site practically and we knew that the war was over then but they had to be real careful because as tricky and sneaky as the Japanese were, they didn't know whether it was going to be another trick or not.

So when we saw the plane come over way, we were really tickled. Then when the war was over, why, we really had a celebration. Those .50 caliber guns, I remember shooting -- and all the big shots on it, they were flying into Manila for the preliminaries, you know, for --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Discussions with MacArthur?

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Right, uh-huh. Because actually -- well, you know, they signed it on the battleship.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That was the Missouri?

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Yes. That was later on, yeah, but they flew in with MacArthur and the rest of the -- General Kruger and General Eikelberger and made all arrangements, preliminary arrangements, yeah, but it was quite a time. So we ended up being out there -- that was like August the 5th, if I remember, '45, so we ended up staying out there with nothing much to do but wait until they called your number to go home. So we was there August, September, October, November -- well, I left there about, I don't know, the 10th of December to go into Manila. Every day or so they would radio a message send private so and so or sergeant so and so, according to how much service, your age, how long you had been in the service, whether you were married, how many points you had, you see, how many trips you made on invasions and so forth, and so that that's how they determined who got to go home first. But it was quite a -- quite a different situation.

Like I say, a lot of people don't realize that there is -- besides the infantry and naval fellas and Air Force pilots and that, there was a lot of fellas that had different jobs that, you know, had a lot to do with the war. We weren't actually there to kill somebody. We were there really to save lives, you see, and that's what ours was. So if you picked up Japanese planes coming in and we were on the coast there of Luzon, like I say, and that's the China Sea and, of course, Japan is right out on the other side so we were facing the right way, well, that's why all four of our units were on the west coast. But it was -- it was quite a -- quite an experience.

We only had trouble once or twice with planes coming in after us, but at that time the Japanese Air Force and that was pretty well whipped. There wasn't too much left of them, you see. But what they were worrying about later on was that they knew that the United States was eventually going to have to invade Japan. In fact, we were -- our platoon was already told that we would be full-time infantry, you know, because there would be no more need for radar. It would be full-time infantry. So needless to say we were pretty damn happy when the war was over. But they were actually shipping fellas from Europe, you know, infantry divisions from Europe that were to go into Japan, so you know what kind of mess that would be. But it was quite an experience, something that a lot of people don't realize happens and so forth but --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing the news when they actually dropped the bomb, the first bomb?

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yes, yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you comprehend what that was?

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: No, no. We couldn't, you know. Just never -- never believed that they would do something. All we could think about was what are we going to do, you know, if they put us in the infantry and what's going to happen to us, you know. Never, never -- I just wonder how many -- well, a lot of officials had to know, but that was a complete surprise. No one had any idea that they were going to do anything like that. It saved a lot of lives. Saved a lot of lives.

Of course, a shame it had to kill 100 or 200,000 Japanese but look how many men we would have lost, and we already lost enough. I think I was reading there on Leyte -- Leyte was probably the sixth largest island in the Philippines and, golly, there was thousands of islands there, and they lost just on the battle of Leyte -- I think they lost a couple of hundred thousand wounded -- I mean killed. I wrote a note at one time I read it, altogether killed and wounded on Leyte was like 12 -- like a 1,200,000, you know. So there was -- the Japanese lost a lot more than that, too, but it was a pretty tough place. By the time they got to Luzon, there wasn't too much left of the Japanese Navy and Air Force and military forces. I think they had pulled back to the homeland, more or less, and expect the invasion, which would have come if they hadn't had the atomic bomb. That's what would have happened. As far as I'm concerned, that's all that could have happened.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have memories of buddies over there?

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Oh, yes, yes. Yes. I lost one good buddy there at Leyte. That's another thing. We came in at night and you might all know, but they dropped us off at a ship out in the harbor and I can remember it was pretty rough out there. The waves were five or six foot high, you had your pack on, you had your gas mask, canteen and I had a B-A-R, a Browning Automatic Rifle, and thank goodness my buddy, he had the ammunition, the tripod for it, but when we went down the roped ladder into the boat, you'd look down and the boat was right there at your feet and by the time you had dropped into the boat, it had dropped with the wave about six foot. I do remember that. Your knees went right up into the back of your ears, all that weight there.

But, yeah, we went in and the one boy, a buddy of mine, he -- I don't know what happened. There was all -- they got hung up on coral and we ended up digging a hole on the beach and sleeping there all night. But the thing I remembered about Leyte was somebody on shore was, say, using a blinker light blinking a message to us and the guys kept saying, Kelch, what are they saying, what are they saying? And I said I don't know what -- what's wrong, but I said we're in trouble. They didn't know whether we were Japs and we didn't know whether they were Japs, that's what the problem was. They weren't sure who we were and we weren't sure whether they were allies or who they were, but that was -- that is one instance I remember quite vaguely. Being their chief radio operator, we had to -- yeah, I had to learn the blinker light and Morse code, also, and I'll still never be able to forget Morse code. I can go through the alphabet just like that and -- but it was quite an experience.

And then after the war we had, like, say three or four months to sit out there and do nothing and they did let us, oh, maybe a half a dozen a time go into Manila and spend a couple of days in there. Manila had been bombed pretty bad. Big beautiful hotels all gone and burnt out. And there wasn't much to do but at least we got in there and we got -- I got some pictures at home of Corregidor. We did take a boat out there and sit on some of the big naval guns and took some pictures. And I thought my land, here we are and here we were a few months ago way out there watching them shell that thing, didn't watch them shell it but all we could see was the flashes of the guns. You know, flashing of the gun. But then --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you dating your wife at the time when you were in the service?

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Or did you meet her after?

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: I dated her before I left for service, yeah, but we corresponded, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right. Was there mail call?

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Oh, yeah, yeah, mail call, yeah, that was -- it was quite a sad time. I mean, if you didn't get mail, it was sad. And if you did, it was a joyous occasion. But that -- you would choke up a lot of times when you would think about times like that. And the one I felt sorry for was the guys -- we had some fellas, our first sergeant, LeHomadu (ps), was from Long Island, New York, and a little Italian fella or French, he was LeHomadu, and -- but he was 38 years old when he was drafted -- when he was inducted in or when he -- I don't know whether he was drafted or whether he joined, but that was the age limit, was 38, so he got -- he got in but he was married.

And to be overseas with married fellas, especially if they had families, you see, and you just couldn't -- you couldn't feel sorry enough for them because you thought you knew how they felt, but if you had never been married, didn't have a family, but you didn't know what they were going through, but it had to have been awfully -- awfully hard for those fellas. I remember when we left San Francisco, we were getting ready to board the ship, when we -- we had to march from -- I don't know how we got -- I don't remember how we got there to the boat, but we had to march probably three or four blocks to the boat, and, yeah, they had us marching like we were in a parade, and a lot of the fellas that were married, the wives had one out there because they could write and tell them where they were. Once you got overseas, you know, your letters were always -- what do you call it -- censored.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Any mail we sent home, it went to Australia, and it was censored there, you see, and they'd cut out anything that they didn't want anyone to know about. But when we were going -- getting ready to board the ship there at San Francisco, a lot of these fellas' wives would be along the way and they would run out and try to, you know, give them a last hug and that and it just really -- I just thought, boy, that's got to be awfully hard for those guys to do. And we got on -- right when we started up the gang plank of the boat, I remembered I wished someone had taken a picture of that big huge banner stretched across an archway there and it says through these portholes passed the best damn soldiers in the world. I remember that.

Yeah. Yeah, it was -- we were young, most of us were young, but we had fellas in our outfit that was 28 and 30 and 35, not too many but enough, that they had a rough time of it because nothing against a service man or the ones that are over in Afghanistan and that now, but they've got -- phones are available to them, they can call home, you know, but once you were over there, you didn't know -- I can remember being up there on the boat watching the shoreline sink in the distance there when we were leaving San Francisco and thinking, you know, how long you're going to be gone and maybe never get back there again, you know. Just think of those fellas who are married and what they were leaving, and I wasn't leaving anything.

I mean, I wasn't married. I had a girlfriend, but I wasn't leaving -- I had two brothers, and they were both in the service so...one brother, he ended up being -- like I said a while ago, we were all three brought up in an orphanage in Cincinnati, and my younger brother was four and I was six and I think my older brother was eight or nine and we were all three in the scouts and we all three loved to do signaling and Morse code. So when we went to Camp Breezy, we all worked on that project, but we all three ended up in the service. And my younger brother was in the Fourth Marine Division in the Pacific and he got in on two or three bad invasions, Saipan and Kwajalein Island and the Marshal Islands, and he was shot up and hit a land mine in a jeep and ended up in naval hospital in Philadelphia for about eight months, if I remember right, thought he was going to be deaf, but he had come out real good, but he had shrapnel through him and through his reproductive organs and had to adopt children, but he was in the signal division. They laid wire. As soon as they hit the shore, they started laying wires for communications. And then the older brother, he ended up being the chief signaler on the U.S.S. Arkansas battleship.

So we all three got a little knowledge in Morse code and signaling in the Boy Scouts, but it's something that the younger generations got to think about; that if there are going to be wars, they'll be wars and they're all going to be different. But this program of taping things like this, I didn't do too much talking about it for years and years but then I figured the kids, my boys, they want to know what's gone on. So this is a good program for them. I don't know what else to say.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, when you think of that experience, does any particularly vivid memory come to mind overseas?

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: I would say to see that Japanese plane fly over with that big red cross marked on it, we knew what it was, that was because as tricky as the Japanese were -- Pearl Harbor is a good example of it -- you didn't know for sure whether they (? mattered ?) or not. But when we saw that, why, it encouraged us being in connection with the main air base, say with radio, we got the news pretty quick, you know, that it was true that the war was over and we would be going home. When, we didn't know, but at least we would be going home in one piece. I don't know much else to say.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you think that covers it?

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: I -- I think we do. I'm just glad to be able to tell the story, to live to tell it, I guess, and it just is great that they can get stories from not just the guys that were right on the frontlines or in the tank car or something like that, but these guys had backed them up. And I told my wife and that about these CBs, these guys that go in and lay these bridges and that even if the fellas what they call Graves Registration Teams, I think they're called the GRT, graves registration, go in and bury the guys or, you know, and a lot of that had to have been a horrible job.

And the medics, you know, was right in there and had to drag the guys back through the jungles and take care of them and have to take care of themselves and watch out for the enemy at the same time, they deserve a lot of credit. But it was -- it was an experience, you know. You're glad you went through it, but you don't ever want it again. No way. No way. No way. We had an Army reunion last September down in -- at Wood Lake and we had eight couples there, eight couples, but we never -- we waited too long after the war to start reunions. But we probably had 15 or 20 of them every year now.

But we lost a lot of fellas, a lot of them were older than we were, but we still have a good time talking about what's happening. But once we got over -- now, when we were in the States, while we would be out on these maneuvers and every so many weeks we would go, like, back into Camp Pinedale and have a chance to meet some of your other buddies in the other platoons, but once we got overseas, why we never saw each other again because one platoon would maybe be in New Guinea someplace and three or four other platoons would be somewhere else, I mean, from the other companies, from the battalion, but there was -- there was three companies, so three companies would have, like, 150 some men. So one company might be in Barnio and one somewhere else, I don't know, but it just so happened that our company was assigned to the Philippines and that's where we ended up and no one saw each other until we started having reunions after the war, which like you say, we waited. But I think a lot of guys just wanted to get it off their mind and get back -- start families and live their life and then they got to thinking about it 50 years later and thought, well, we ought to get together and talk things over.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Is that what your installation would look like then in that picture?

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Yeah, yeah. Uh-hum. Yeah, that's -- like you see, they have their tents all camouflaged here. These stuck out -- didn't stick out quite as much as they do there. They had them camouflaged paint on them like so according to which way the -- yeah, you see, that was the radar antenna and this is probably the vans in here that had their operating equipment and then our radio was set up usually a couple of hundred yards away and maybe be in a tent or in a -- you know, we were hooked up for the 13th Air Force once we got the Signal Corps was with -- once we got overseas but here it tells about something about the air warning battalions and so forth, but it was -- it was a different kind of duty, but everybody had their own stories.

I'm just looking up here at the unit book I got from the VFW. Those are my two brothers and I. That's when we went into the children's home. That's all we had: A box. Yup. That's all we had was a box. Here was this -- I thought this -- I was looking some of this up. I thought it was going to show -- this is Biak Island that we was on, but I thought it was going to show some of the caves, but they didn't have too much of it. I just went through some of this. This General Eikelberger, he was head of the Eighth Army in the Pacific. He was from Urbana.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Oh, yeah. He's right out the edge of town. There's a big two-story big house with a hell of a big lot on it right out the edge of town and that was the Eikelberger home. Yeah, he was from Urbana. As a matter of fact, in New Guinea, he had -- one of his groups he called it the Urbana force. Yeah. And like I said, he was in charge of the Sixth Army in the Pacific. They had the Sixth and Eighth Armys over there. And they had some of these -- I don't know what this is here. Now here you see this is the way that those LSTs would look going into -- this was the invasion of Leyte right here, you see, and this kamikaze pilots had me scared and I didn't go down and sleep downstairs.

I crawled underneath one of these big two-and-a-half ton trucks and I just had room to put my Army cot under there and sleep there. I figured if anything had come off, buddy, I wasn't going to be down below deck. Here is a map of the Philippines here. These are the bigger islands. Here was Leyte way down here. Here is the Mindoro, that's the island we laid all out under the smoke screen. And then Subic Bay is -- that's Manila Bay right there, and then Subic Bay is a little place way up in here, so we were -- that's Lingayen, that was in town, not no big city, but we were between there and Subic Bay right here, this little town right in there. So we had four platoons cover that whole west coast of Luzon there. There's Corregidor.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Wow. My goodness.

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Well, I think that gives you some idea of what --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Good. Yes. Excellent.

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: What -- well, somebody will have sometime to get some information out of what -- have you interviewed quite a few different --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Oh, yes (inaudible). I've -- yes, I've talked to -- I've lost track -- more than a hundred Veterans.

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Oh, really?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Yes. I've submitted 80 to the Library of Congress now and there are probably 30 tapes that I'm putting together to send this summer.

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Oh, my goodness.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And, yeah. So, I mean, I've talked to quite a few.

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well, I guess we're coming up on almost two years now. I've been doing it since April of 2001. Heard about it when my uncle showed me a story from a VFW magazine.

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: VFW has been running fairly regular stories about it.

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: They have, yeah. I keep thinking about it and I keep thinking, you know, how will I do it and I'll do it and --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Here is your souvenir pamphlet.

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Oh, thank you, thank you. Thank you.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That tells you about the whole thing.

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Oh, good. Good.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Because the project is for Veterans of all wars.

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But I've just been doing World War II.

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: So mine is strictly with World War II guys.

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: My dad was in World War II, so I've always been interested in it.

sp.speaker: Orlando Kelch
sp.p: Well, good. Good.
(End of interview)
